counties.heading: What it takes to put a measure on your county's ballot
counties.intro: California Elections Code §9118 sets the bar for a county initiative at 10% of the votes cast for all candidates for Governor at the last gubernatorial election. Not 10% of residents, and not 10% of registered voters — 10% of the people who actually turned out.
counties.example: In Sonoma County that is 19,746 signatures. The figure is not a target anyone invented: it is the size of the group that can already put a question on the ballot where you live, whether or not that group is you.

modes.shareHint: How large the requirement is next to the county's electorate.
modes.peopleHint: Signatures required, on a logarithmic scale — the raw counts span four orders of magnitude.

rail.selectPrompt: Select a county to see what it requires.
rail.sourceLink: California Secretary of State, Statement of Vote

framing.heading: What a low number does and does not mean
framing.body: A county where fewer signatures are needed is not an easier target. It is a county where a small organised group already decides what reaches the ballot — whether or not that group is you. Low turnout does not create an opening so much as describe who is currently holding one.

footnote.heading: The details that matter
footnote.statute: The 10% requirement is set by <0>California Elections Code §9118</0>.
footnote.specialElection: A petition signed by 20% of that same number compels a special election, rather than waiting for the next regular one.
footnote.notPassing: Qualifying a measure is not passing one. These figures put a question to the voters; they decide it.
footnote.cities: Cities work differently. A general-law city sets its bar at 10% of its registered voters, not of votes cast, and a charter city sets its own.
footnote.verify: Every figure here links to the public record it came from. Check it.
